The earnings week the last three reports kept warning about arrived, and it split the book exactly along the line those warnings drew. Five positions went into it. KO gapped straight through its stop on its print — filled 94.24, stopped 91.53, opened 90.82 on 10-27 — for −1.08R, the worst position in the record. AAPL was trailed out at −0.64R the day before its own. The two that held came out as free runners: ABBV reached T1 on its earnings morning for +0.75R banked and XOM is +1.69R with its stop 8.15 above the fill. Total R rose to 4.41R and equity to $52,185, but realised R fell from 2.69 to 1.72R, because the week banked two large losses and one T1.

Account equity — the same record in money

R is a risk multiple: 1R = $500, a fixed 1% of the starting account, and it stays fixed whether the account is up or down. The curve below is the same record converted to money — real share counts, real fills, real exits, marked to the close every session. The two views agree to $20 across 23 positions; the gap is share rounding, because a position sized int($500 / risk) almost never risks exactly $500.

The shape is the part worth looking at. The account made money steadily for a month, peaked at $54,230 on 2026-10-02, then gave back $2,814 into the 10-08 squeeze — 5.19% from the peak, or 5.63% of the account. It has recovered about half of that since. Both squeezes cost real money and the record still ends up ahead, which is the only test that matters.

How to read it. Realised to date and Open at the close are running totals, so every row satisfies $50,000 + realised + open = equity. Equity change is the week-on-week move and mixes the two: a week can bank profit and still lose equity if the open book gave back more, which is what happened to 10-09. Banked that week is realised money only, and the events beside it sum to it exactly — a T1 tag is half a position sold while the rest keeps running, which is money in the account even though the trade is still open.

Does adding to a winner help? — the rule tested, not asserted

Correction — I had this backwards. An earlier build of this report said adding to MCD would have turned a +1.48R winner into a +0.23R scratch. That number came from a bug, not from the market: the add was being evaluated before the stop check on the same bar, so an add made late in the 09-23 session retro-actively raised a stop that price had already taken out earlier that morning. With the bar processed in the correct order, adding is better, not worse.

The argmax moved this week, which is the strongest argument against chasing it. A week ago the best setting over twelve positions was a +0.00R gate. Re-swept over fourteen, the top is now a plateau: +0.25R and +0.50R tie at +8.47R, with +0.00R 0.22R behind. The rule has been moved to the conservative end of that plateau, +0.25R, and the reason is concrete rather than statistical: the add a +0.00R gate allowed and a +0.25R gate refused was AAPL on 09-21 at +0.23R — a position that went on to stop out. Requiring a trade to be meaningfully in profit before adding is not a curve fit; it is the difference between adding to something that is working and adding to something that merely has not failed yet.
And it breaches the risk cap. Simulated forward, the adopted rule carries $3,245 of open heat — 6.5% — and with this week's two new shorts that is 8.5%, through the 10% ceiling and well through the 8.5% event-week ceiling. NKE reaches 412 shares three sessions before it reports. The extra R is not free; it is bought with size, and the caps below are what stop that size arriving all at once.

Seven adds in a one-way tape is not proof. Every one was made into a position that kept going, in a month where the average stock fell while the index did not. That is evidence the rule behaves correctly in a trend — not evidence it is safe in a choppy one, where the raised stop is exactly what gets hit. The live book below is not rewritten: no report ever published an add, so none was taken, and every position you hold is single size. The rule applies from next week.

What has actually been learned

A stop is not protection against an event. KO is the clean experiment: the position was sized to lose $500 and lost $537, because the stock opened 0.71 below the stop. That is a 7% overrun on one gap, and it is the smallest version of this failure — a worse print would have opened further down with the same stop. Four reports in a row said the only decision that helps is the one taken before the print. This is what it costs when it is not taken.

And yet holding through earnings was right twice out of four. ABBV and XOM both reported inside the window and both came out as free runners; KO and AAPL did not survive. That is a coin flip with a real cost attached, which is the argument for the earnings filter rather than against it — not that prints are bad, but that a 3–15 day swing has no edge in them.

The first add since 10-06 is approved this week. NFLX clears the +0.25R gate with a re-issue beyond the fill, no print, and heat to spare. Adds remain -1.07R across the record, so this is leverage being taken deliberately in a tape that supports it, not a free improvement. The stop on the whole position moves so combined risk stays at 1R.

A position was cut for failing the screen rather than for losing money. FAST is −0.42R, inside the −0.5R cut line, but its relative-strength percentile slipped to 68 against the 70 the trend template requires. It is a marginal fail on one session. It is still a fail, and the rule is not re-litigated per position — that is the whole point of having written it down in advance.

The long book is still the weak half and the gap is still widening. Ten longs have produced -1.91R against 6.32R from thirteen shorts. But the two best positions in the book right now are both longs, both free, and both found by the same screen that produced the losers. The difference between them is not the screen; it is that these two were given room to run.

Twenty-three positions, eighteen closed, 1.72R banked ($+866), 4.41R total. Account equity $52,185, 4.37% on a $50,000 start. Seven of twenty-three positions have reached T1; none has reached T2 in eight weeks.

The logic, stated as rules

Every filter below is computed from split-adjusted daily OHLCV — nothing is discretionary, and nothing was chosen after seeing which names would pass. The rule set fuses four published frameworks: Weinstein's stage analysis for the regime a stock is in, Minervini's trend template for whether it is in a genuine Stage 2 advance, the Donchian / Turtle channel breakout for the trigger, and volatility contraction plus volume signature for whether the base is being accumulated or merely drifting.

Long — Stage 2 trend template (all seven must be true)

  1. Moving-average stack. Close > 50 SMA > 150 SMA > 200 SMA, and close above all three.
  2. Slope. 200 SMA higher than 21 sessions ago and 50 SMA higher than 10 sessions ago — the trend is being renewed, not decaying.
  3. Proximity to high. Within 25% of the 52-week high. Leadership does not hide in the bottom of its range.
  4. Distance from low. At least 25% above the 52-week low — filters out dead-cat bounces off a Stage 4 base.
  5. Relative strength. RS in the top 30% of the universe, where RS is the IBD-style weighted excess return over SPY: 40% × 3-month, 20% each × 6-, 9- and 12-month.
  6. Liquidity. 20-day average dollar volume ≥ $50M, so a 10–40 share-lot or a spread fills without slippage.
  7. Base structure. Range depth ≤ 18% measured over the shortest of the last 25, 40 or 60 sessions that qualifies.

Long — setup trigger (base rules plus these)

  • Proximity to pivot. Price within 7% of the base high — close enough that a buy stop is a trade, not a hope.
  • Not extended. No more than 14% above the 50 SMA. A stock already 3–5 ATR extended is a bad breakout buy regardless of how good the trend looks.
  • Volatility contraction or accumulation. Either ATR% today ≤ its level 20 sessions ago, or ATR% ≤ 0.85× its level 40 sessions ago (the VCP signature); or up-volume ÷ down-volume over 20 sessions ≥ 0.95.

Short — Stage 4 breakdown (all six must be true)

  1. Inverted stack. Close below both the 50 SMA and 200 SMA, and 50 SMA below 200 SMA.
  2. Slope. 200 SMA or 50 SMA declining — supply is in control on at least one timeframe.
  3. Proximity to low. No more than 25% above the 52-week low.
  4. Damage done. At least 18% below the 52-week high — this is a broken stock, not a pullback in an uptrend.
  5. Relative weakness. RS in the bottom 30% of the universe.
  6. Distribution. Up-volume ÷ down-volume over 20 sessions ≤ 1.05 — rallies are not being bought.

Trigger adds: price within 7% above the 25/40/60-session base low, and not more than 14% below the 50 SMA (an already-collapsed stock mean-reverts violently and is a poor short entry).

Entry, stop and target construction

  • Entry. Stop order at the structural pivot — the higher of the base high and the 20-day Donchian high for longs, the lower of the base low and the 20-day Donchian low for shorts — plus a 0.10 ATR buffer through the level. No anticipation, no limit orders inside the base.
  • Stop. The wider of the nearest structural level (10-day extreme, base extreme, or nearest clustered S/R zone) offset by 0.30 ATR, capped at 2.2 ATR from entry. The Turtle system's 2N stop, with structure allowed to tighten it but never to widen it past 2.2N.
  • Target 1. Entry ± 1.5R. Take a third to a half off; move the stop to breakeven.
  • Target 2. The measured move — base height projected from the pivot — or 2.8R, whichever is further.
  • Trail. Once a position is on it is managed by this report every week, and the stop ratchets one way only. Each week the managed stop is the tightest of: the stop already in force; the 5-day Donchian extreme in the opposite direction offset by 0.25 ATR (horizon-matched to a 3–15 day swing, where the Turtle 20-day exit is far too loose); the price that caps remaining give-back at 1R; and the original fill once the trade is +1.0R or better. It is then floored 0.75 ATR away from the last close so it never sits inside the noise band. A re-issued stop can tighten risk on a live trade but can never widen it.
  • Sizing. Shares = $500 ÷ (entry − stop), capped at 30% of account notional per position.
  • Book heat. Total risk across every position — open, added-to and new — is capped at 15% of the account, cut to 13.5% in any week where a live position reports earnings inside the holding window. Heat is spent in a fixed order: positions flagged to cut are closed first and their risk freed, open positions keep theirs, then adds, then new entries in score order. Anything that does not fit is deferred with its levels intact, not deleted.

How open positions are tracked

  • One position per symbol and side. The first plan to trigger opens the position. Every later week's plan for the same symbol and side is a management update — a revised stop and revised targets on the trade already on — not a second trade. Grading each week's plan file as an independent cohort double-counts every carried position, and that is exactly what the earlier scorecards in this series did.
  • Selection is a union, never a filter. The weekly book is this week's screen picks plus every still-open position. The sector cap, the breadth rule and the setup-ready filter govern new entries only. None of them may drop a live position out of the book, because the result is a real position running with a stale stop that nobody is watching. The build fails if any open position lacks a card.
  • Re-entry is allowed, repetition is not. Once a position closes the symbol goes flat, and only a plan issued after the close date may open a new one — so the book never re-enters on the same stale level twice.
  • T1 takes half off, it does not close the position. Half comes off at Target 1 and books 0.75R; the balance rides the same daily trail toward Target 2 with its stop moved to at least breakeven. Booking the whole position at T1 caps every winner at exactly 1.5R while every loser is free to run to −1R, and the trail is what is supposed to pay for the losers.
  • Adding to a position that is working. A position is added to when this week's plan re-issues the same side at a trigger beyond the fill and the position is already through the gate. Half a unit per add, at most two per position. After an add the stop on the whole position moves so combined open risk stays at 1R of the original unit — an add can never turn a winner into more than a 1R loser. Never add back after Target 1 has been taken: scaling out and buying back in are two decisions that cancel, with two lots of slippage.
  • What blocks an add. Four separate guards, any one of which is enough: the name reports earnings inside the holding window; breadth is below 40% and the add is on the long side, because adding shares to a long is owning more long exposure and the no-new-longs rule covers it; the name no longer passes its side of the screen; or the add does not fit under the book heat cap. Heat is spent in a fixed order — positions flagged to cut are closed first and their risk freed, open positions keep theirs, then adds, then new entries in score order. Anything that does not fit is deferred with its levels intact, not deleted.
  • Why adds rank ahead of new entries. Adding to a position that is already working is a higher-probability use of the same risk than a fresh trigger that may never fill — roughly a third of planned triggers never do.

How the levels on each chart were derived

  • Swing highs / lows. Fractal pivots — a bar whose high is the strict maximum (or low the strict minimum) of the five bars either side of it. Marked ▼ and ▲ on the charts.
  • Support / resistance zones. Three-bar fractal pivots from the last 15 months, clustered where they fall within 0.6 ATR of each other. Each zone carries a touch count and the date it was last tested — a level touched four times is a different object from one touched once.
  • Volume profile. Six months of daily bars, 80 price bins, each bar's volume distributed uniformly across its high–low range. POC is the highest-volume bin; the value area is the 70% of volume around it; HVN are local maxima above the 75th percentile (shaded purple — price tends to stall and rotate there); LVN are local minima below the 25th percentile (grey dotted — price tends to move through them quickly).
  • Donchian channels. 20-day and 55-day extremes, excluding the current bar.

Sources

Minervini trend template criteria — Deepvue, TraderLion on stage analysis. Donchian breakout lengths, the N/ATR volatility unit, 2N stop and 20-day trailing exit — the original Turtle trading rules. Volume-profile HVN/LVN/POC methodology — AlgoVistra, FXOpen on fixed-range volume profile. Price data via Yahoo Finance; live quotes, option chains, Greeks and the earnings calendar via the connected brokerage MCP.

Market regime

The split between the index and its members is now extreme. SPY fell to 755.72, a third week below its 50-day (767.49) and -3.31% off its high. QQQ is worse: 690.49, -6.95% over a month and -9.49% off its high. Against that, breadth rose again from 56.5% to 59.5%, the fifth consecutive weekly gain, and the share above the 200-day reached 64.3%. Stage 2 holds at 16.1% against Stage 4 at 13.7%. VIX is unchanged at 19.42. Three in five stocks are above their own 50-day while the index that contains them cannot get back above its own.

The long screen has never been stronger and the short screen has never been more extended. 27 longs pass with 23 setup-ready, the most of the series, and the accumulation readings are extraordinary: KDP 3.42, MA 3.23, CCEP 2.81, V 2.77, ABBV 2.64. Sixteen of them are within 3% of a 52-week high. The short screen still has 23 passers but only 9 are setup-ready, and the leaders are at the bottom of their ranges — BKNG 1.3% above its 52-week low, TTWO 3.4%, BA 4.0%. Shorting a name that has already fallen a third into a tape where three in five stocks are rising is where squeezes are made. So both new entries are long, no new short is taken, and the best short on the board is carried as a watch card.

What the leadership is telling you

Earnings season is over and it changed the shape of the screen. Three weeks ago every candidate reported inside the window; this week only APP does, in the entire book. Sixteen of the twenty-three setup-ready longs have a clean calendar. The constraint that picked the last two weeks' entries has lifted, and what is left is the ranking itself.

Leadership is defensives, payments and energy — and it is being bought, not drifting up. ABBV 79.3 (up/down 2.64), CVX 78.9 (2.06), TMO 77.9, XOM 77.6 (2.34), KDP 77.6 (3.42), KO 77.3 (1.82), MNST 76.9 (2.47), V 76.0 (2.77). An up/down volume above 2.0 means twice as much volume on up days as down days; eight names on this screen are above 2.0 and none of them is a megacap technology stock.

What would change the read. Breadth has risen five weeks running, from 31.4% to 59.5%. The thing to watch is no longer whether the rotation is real — it plainly is — but whether the index catching down to its members matters more than its members catching up. A week where breadth falls and SPY stays below its 50-day would say the former.

Why some high scorers were not given plans

Three filters sit on top of the ranking. Sector concentration — the two-per-sector cap counts open positions. Extension — names more than 14% below their 50-day are refused because that is where squeezes start. Setup-ready only — fourteen of the twenty-three short passers fail a trigger condition.

With earnings no longer binding, the choice came down to sector and correlation. CVX (78.9) was refused because XOM is already held and they are one oil trade; TMO (77.9) was refused because ABBV is already held; MA (72.3) was refused because it is the same payments trade as V, which scores higher. KO is a re-entry: it is the name that gapped through its stop on 10-27, has since recovered the whole gap, and now carries no event. On the short side the screen is extended rather than weak, so PCAR — the best distribution reading on the board at 0.41 — is prepared as a watch card instead of taken.

Long plans — breakout / trend continuation

Five long cards — three live, one cut, one new. XOM and ABBV are past Target 1 with stops above their fills and are management-only. FAST is flagged to close: it no longer passes the trend template. KO is a re-entry at a trigger above the fill that gapped out on its earnings morning, with the print now behind it. V is the first financial this book has held. This week's decisions, in order

  • 1. Close FAST. 181 shares at the market. It fails the trend template on relative strength (68 against a 70 minimum). This is a screen decision, not a loss decision.
  • 2. Move the open stops to the "stop for Monday" figure: XOM 179.16, ABBV 281.95, APP 257.28, NFLX 65.99 — or 66.10 if you place the add.
  • 3. Place the add on NFLX — 53 shares at 61.20, taking the position to 160 at a 62.99 average. The stop on the whole position then moves to 66.10. If you skip the add, keep the 107 shares and the 65.99 stop; both are consistent books.
  • 4. Place the two longs. KO 95.53 buy stop, 139 shares, or five Dec-18 95/100 call spreads for $955. V 417.72 buy stop, 31 shares, no option.
  • 5. Decide about APP before Wednesday. +1.07R with a free stop and a print on 11-04. The choices are flat before it, hedged through it, or accept gap risk on the open profit. The one choice that is not available is relying on the stop.
  • 6. Leave XOM and ABBV alone. Both are past T1, both lock profit, both are blocked from adds by rule. XOM’s remaining 30 shares cannot finish below +1.01R.
  • No new shorts. The short screen's leaders sit 1–4% above their 52-week lows while three in five stocks are above their own 50-day. PCAR has the best distribution reading on either screen and is still only a watch card.

Execution notes

  • Monday 2026-11-02 is the next session — a normal week. If a stock gaps through its trigger by more than 0.5 ATR, stand aside.
  • The one new structure expires 2026-12-18, 46 DTE — inside the usual 35–55 band for the first time in a month, because there is no longer an earnings calendar to price around.
  • KO has the best chain in the report. The 95 call quotes 2.21 / 2.29 on 9,154 open interest with 990 traded — a 3.6% spread — and the 100 leg shows 3,373 open. Five spreads cost $955 and risk $495 at the underlying stop.
  • V is shares only, and the reason is the short leg rather than the long one: 313 contracts open at 440 and 575 at 435, both under the 800 this report requires of a leg it intends to sell.
  • The stop ratchet is one-way. If a revised stop looks wider than what you already have working, keep yours. That applies to the NFLX add too — 66.10 is tighter than 66.65.
  • Re-run the scan on any 2%+ index day. With SPY three weeks under its 50-day and VIX at 19.42, that remains live.

What would invalidate this whole report

The standing invalidation did not fire. VIX closed at 19.42, below the 22 line, with SPY below its 50-day (767.49). One leg holds, the other does not, as it has for three weeks.

What would make the long thesis wrong. Breadth falling while SPY stays below its 50-day. It has risen five weeks running — 31.4%, 42.3%, 45.8%, 56.5%, 59.5% — and the 200-day reading is now 64.3%. A single down week in breadth would be the first real evidence that the index is leading and the members are late.

What would make the shorts wrong. APP is 1.5% above its 52-week low and NFLX 1.1% above its own. Both are deeply profitable and both are where a squeeze does the most damage. The add on NFLX makes this worse by design: more size at a tighter stop. That is the trade-off the add rule was adopted with, and it is the reason it is capped at two.

The one dated risk is APP on 11-04. Everything else in the book is clean through the holding window for the first time since late September.
